title: Mia, an AI reader of screening mammograms, flags a 6 mm cancer that NHS Grampian radiologists missed, and the patient needs only surgery and five days of radiotherapy
summary: In NHS Grampian's GEMINI evaluation, Mia flagged a 6 mm breast cancer that radiologists had missed in a patient named Barbara, and she had surgery and needed only five days of radiotherapy.
account: Mia, an AI mammography reader by Kheiron Medical Technologies, was used alongside radiologists in National Health Service (NHS) Grampian's GEMINI breast-screening evaluation. It covered 10,889 women in Aberdeen, Scotland, who were screened between 27 February and 5 October 2023. Dr Gerald Lip, clinical director of breast screening at NHS Grampian, led the evaluation. On 21 March 2024 BBC News described Barbara, an Aberdeen patient. She was one of 11 women whose cancer Mia flagged and hospital radiologists had not spotted on the scan. Her 6 mm tumor was caught so early that she had an operation and needed only five days of radiotherapy. The date of Barbara's screening is not given. A University of Aberdeen statement the same day said that Mia helped find 12% more cancers than routine practice. In the peer-reviewed GEMINI paper, published in Nature Cancer on 10 March 2026, Clarisse de Vries, Gerald Lip and colleagues report the screening dates. They confirm that 11 additional cancers were found with Mia, seven of them invasive and four ductal carcinoma in situ. They report that three-year follow-up for interval cancers was not yet available. Three of the authors were Kheiron employees, and the authors state that the vendor could not access the workspace where the analysis was run.
purpose: Mia was built to read screening mammograms and flag suspicious findings alongside human readers. Detecting a cancer that readers missed is its intended function.
segment: AI reader in population mammography screening

ratings.reason: A 6 mm cancer was treated at an early stage with surgery and a short radiotherapy course. Dr Lip states that cancers picked up under 15 mm carry around 95% survival. The benefit is potentially life-saving but not demonstrated as such for this patient.
Across the 10,889-woman evaluation Mia helped find 12% more cancers. The University of Aberdeen statement says this would not put more women through additional tests.

ai_role.statement: Mia flagged a lesion that the hospital radiologists had not identified on the same scan. Clinicians then confirmed and treated the cancer. Both the BBC and the University of Aberdeen attribute the detection to Mia. The counterfactual is that the cancer would have been found later, at a larger size, rather than never.

Cohort detection gains and general survival figures are different claims.

fields.summary: In NHS Grampian's GEMINI evaluation, Mia flagged a 6 mm breast cancer that radiologists had missed in a patient named Barbara, and she had surgery and needed only five days of radiotherapy.
fields.account: Mia, an AI mammography reader by Kheiron Medical Technologies, was used alongside radiologists in National Health Service (NHS) Grampian's GEMINI breast-screening evaluation. It covered 10,889 women in Aberdeen, Scotland, who were screened between 27 February and 5 October 2023. Dr Gerald Lip, clinical director of breast screening at NHS Grampian, led the evaluation. On 21 March 2024 BBC News described Barbara, an Aberdeen patient. She was one of 11 women whose cancer Mia flagged and hospital radiologists had not spotted on the scan. Her 6 mm tumor was caught so early that she had an operation and needed only five days of radiotherapy. The date of Barbara's screening is not given. A University of Aberdeen statement the same day said that Mia helped find 12% more cancers than routine practice. In the peer-reviewed GEMINI paper, published in Nature Cancer on 10 March 2026, Clarisse de Vries, Gerald Lip and colleagues report the screening dates. They confirm that 11 additional cancers were found with Mia, seven of them invasive and four ductal carcinoma in situ. They report that three-year follow-up for interval cancers was not yet available. Three of the authors were Kheiron employees, and the authors state that the vendor could not access the workspace where the analysis was run.
